lead: 3D manipulation lets a user select a virtual object and change its position, orientation or size. The task is what changes; the technique is how the user changes it; the constraint is what motion is allowed. Good manipulation keeps the hand-to-object mapping predictable, adds constraints so motion stays useful, and gives feedback at once. It is used in VR design reviews, surgical rehearsal, AR furniture placement and telerobotics. This chapter separates task, technique and constraint, then gives the ray-selection calculation and the main design rules.
prereq: You need: input device characteristics from Unit 2 and transformation matrices from Unit 4; the scene-graph view of transforms is in 5.4.

sections.h3: Manipulation tasks and degrees of freedom

blocks.text: 3D manipulation has two parts: the task and the technique. The task says what must change. Selection identifies an object. Translation changes position. Rotation changes orientation. Scaling changes size. A full rigid object has six degrees of freedom, 6 DOF: three translations along x, y, z and three rotations about x, y, z.

Degrees of freedom (DOF) count the independent quantities a user can change. A door hinge is a 1 DOF rotation. A slider on a rail is a 1 DOF translation. Dragging on a table top is a 2 DOF task. Scaling adds up to three values, one per axis. More DOF gives freedom but makes control harder.

A constraint removes some DOF: lock motion to an axis, to a surface or to a plane. Snap replaces continuous motion with fixed steps, such as a 0.10 m grid or 15° rotation steps. Constraints and snap make precise placement possible with a noisy hand tracker.
The user confirms the change by releasing a trigger, pressing a button or making a gesture. Until confirmation, the object is held. Undo must be available because a wrong transform is easy to make.

sections.h3: Techniques: direct hand, ray, Go-Go and HOMER

blocks.text: Direct virtual hand maps the tracked hand position to a virtual hand. The object follows when the hand touches it. It is natural for objects within arm reach. It fails for distant objects.

Ray casting shoots a ray from the hand or controller. The ray selects the first object it hits. After selection, the user can pull the object along the ray, or attach it and then move. Ray casting works at a distance but gives poor depth judgement.
t = (c − p)·u,  q = p + t u,  d = ||c − q||
blocks.where: p is the ray origin, u is the unit ray direction, c is the object centre, t is the projection along the ray, q is the closest point on the ray, and d is the perpendicular distance from the ray to c. A sphere of radius R is selected when t ≥ 0 and d ≤ R.

blocks.text: Go-Go extends reach with a threshold D_th and gain k. For real hand distance D_r from the tracking origin, the virtual hand distance is D_v = D_r when D_r ≤ D_th, and D_v = D_th + k(D_r − D_th) when D_r > D_th. Beyond the threshold the virtual hand moves faster than the real hand.

HOMER combines ray selection and hand manipulation. The user selects with a ray, then the object attaches to the hand at a fixed offset. Moving the hand moves the object with better control than ray dragging. The offset must stay constant, otherwise the object jumps at pick-up.

sections.h3: World-in-miniature, props, haptics and design rules

blocks.text: World-in-miniature (WIM) shows a small copy of the whole scene in front of the user. The user moves the miniature object or the miniature viewpoint; the change applies to the full-size world. WIM is good for large scenes and for objects out of reach. The mental mapping between small and large must be clear.

Props are tracked physical objects, such as a pen, a handle or a cube. A haptic handle adds force feedback, so the user feels a stop at a limit or the weight of a tool. Props reduce fatigue because the arm can rest, and they give passive haptic cues. They need calibration to the virtual object.

Two-handed manipulation uses one hand to anchor or select and the other to rotate or scale. This is useful for inspection and assembly. Design rules: give immediate visual feedback (highlight, ghost, shadow); set gain so small hand motions make large object motions only when needed; use a threshold or dead zone to stop jitter; avoid long mid-air holds that tire the shoulder; keep the mapping between hand and object stable.

Input device choice follows Unit 2. A 6 DOF controller suits 6 DOF transforms; a data glove suits direct hand interaction; a haptic device suits guided assembly. Usability checks for these choices are in 5.8.

figure.caption: The ray-selection test with the worked example's own numbers: t = 2.00 m along the ray gives the closest point q, and the perpendicular distance d = 0.10 m is what decides selection. Because 0.10 m is under the sphere radius 0.15 m, the ray selects the sphere.

spec.title: Ray test: d = 0.10 m < R = 0.15 m
spec.aria: A six-step chain: from ray origin p and centre c, compute the offset w, project it to get t = 2.00 m, find the closest point q, get the perpendicular distance d = 0.10 m, and compare it with the sphere radius 0.15 m to see that the ray selects the sphere.

examples.question: A controller ray starts at (0, 0, 0) and points along (0, 0, −1). A sphere has centre (0.10, 0, −2.00) m and radius 0.15 m. Find the perpendicular distance from the ray to the centre and say whether the ray selects the sphere.
steps: Ray origin p = (0, 0, 0), unit direction u = (0, 0, −1), sphere centre c = (0.10, 0, −2.00) m, radius R = 0.15 m.
Vector from ray origin to centre: w = c − p = (0.10, 0, −2.00) m.
Projection along the ray: t = w·u = 0.10×0 + 0×0 + (−2.00)×(−1) = 2.00 m. t is positive, so the centre is in front of the ray.
Closest point on the ray: q = p + t u = (0, 0, 0) + 2.00(0, 0, −1) = (0, 0, −2.00) m.
Offset from the ray to the centre: c − q = (0.10, 0, 0) m.
Compare d = 0.10 m with R = 0.15 m. d ≤ R, so the ray intersects the sphere and selects it.
examples.answer: The perpendicular distance is 0.10 m; the ray selects the sphere because 0.10 m < 0.15 m.
examples.check:
import math
p = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)
u = (0.0, 0.0, -1.0)
c = (0.10, 0.0, -2.00)
R = 0.15
w = tuple(c[i] - p[i] for i in range(3))
t = sum(w[i] * u[i] for i in range(3))
q = tuple(p[i] + t * u[i] for i in range(3))
d = math.sqrt(sum((c[i] - q[i]) ** 2 for i in range(3)))
print(t)
print(d)
print(R)

traps: Ray selection tests perpendicular distance d, not the distance t along the ray. A far object on the ray can be selected; a near object off the ray cannot.
6 DOF means three translations plus three rotations. Scaling is a separate transform with up to three values.
Go-Go is 1:1 only up to the threshold; beyond it the gain k applies.
HOMER keeps a fixed offset after ray selection; the object is not dragged by the ray for the whole task.
A constraint limits motion; snap forces discrete values. They solve different precision problems.

quiz.a: Changing three translations along x, y, z and three rotations about x, y, z.

quiz.q: Why add an axis constraint when turning a virtual valve?
quiz.a: The valve needs rotation about one axis only. The constraint removes wrong translations and tilts, so the hand tracker noise does not move the valve off its mount.

quiz.q: A ray starts at (0, 0, 0) and points along (0, 1, 0). A sphere has centre (0.20, 3.00, 0) m and radius 0.10 m. Find t and d, and say whether the ray selects it.
Go-Go has threshold D_th = 0.30 m, gain k = 2.5, and real hand distance D_r = 0.50 m. Find the virtual hand distance D_v.
Compare direct virtual hand and ray casting for an object 3 m away.
quiz.a: Direct hand cannot reach 3 m, so it needs Go-Go or a WIM. Ray casting reaches 3 m but gives weak depth judgement for placing the object along the ray. Ray selection plus hand manipulation, as in HOMER, is better.

quiz.q: What problem does a world-in-miniature solve?
quiz.a: It gives the user a reachable copy of a large or distant scene, so objects outside arm reach can be selected and moved through the miniature.

quiz.q: Why can a long mid-air hold cause fatigue, and what design change helps?
quiz.a: Holding the arm against gravity tires the shoulder. A prop, an arm rest, a lower gain or a confirm-on-release design shortens the hold and supports the arm.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer work uses hand tracking without controllers, eye tracking for selection, haptic retargeting and redirected touching to align a real prop with a virtual object. Industrial digital twins use these techniques for remote assembly and training. Search for 3D manipulation taxonomies, Go-Go interaction, HOMER remote manipulation and haptic retargeting.
